newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac says will be happy to receive Blair.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says will be happy to receive Blair.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said in a message on Friday to British election victor Tony Blair that he would be happy to meet him soon in the French capital.

"As you know, I always take into account with the deepest interest Britain's positions on (European) questions and I would be very happy to receive you soon to start a confident dialogue on all subjects of common interest," Chirac wrote according to his office.

The message was not a formal invitation nor were exact dates mentioned. But specialists said it was widely expected there would be a high-level contact between France and Britain's new Labour administration once it formally took office.
Chirac, congratulating Blair for his "outstanding success", recalled they had met during the French leader's visit to Britain last year and established friendly personal relations.
Chirac added that he strongly believed in Franco-British cooperation and that he hoped it would grow, especially concerning further moves dealing with Europe.

The French leader sent a message to outgoing premier John Major praising him for his role in strengthening ties between Paris and London and offering his best wishes "for the new stage that lies ahead for you."
Prime Minister Alain Juppe predicted "very good relations" with Blair, and said his victory mean a greater British openness towards Europe, especially in the social sector.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin sent Blair a brief congratulatory message saying he "rejoiced the British people had changed majority in order to change their future." The campaign slogan of France's Socialists in the country's current general election campaign is "Let's change future."
Communist party chief Robert Hue said the election result was satisfying but that he doubted Blair would carry out major changes to Britain's economic and social policies."

The left-wing French reaction was accompanied by a statement from Michel Barnier, European Affairs Minister in Chirac's centre-right government who said the Socialists had yet to understand their British counterparts won the election because they had dropped "outmoded precepts" about state control of the economy.

Labour won because Britain's public had enough of "conservative men and ideas" but in France it was the Socialists who were the conservatives "...because they have not made the changes (to their ideology) that Tony Blair and Labour made.

"The British Labour victory was also because of the intelligence of a man and his party (Tony Blair and Labour) who were smart enough to throw into the Thames certain outmoded precepts about the state having to run the economy and who also made their choice for Europe," Barnier told Radio Monte Carlo.
France's Socialists still believe strongly in government intervention in economic affairs.

"What we also saw in Britain, as in Italy, Spain and certain German regions - and I hope we will see in France at election time in a few weeks - is the defeat of all those who have always said 'it's Brussels' fault', 'it's Maastricht's fault,"' he said.
Barnier was referring to increasing concern among some French Socialist leaders at the rapid pace of European integration, which they saw as being increasingly weighted in favour of big business.
"I have the impression that Tony Blair perfectly understood that his place was in Europe, not next to Europe or behind it, but squarely in front," Barnier said.

"On many topics, the new Labour government will have men who want to play a key role in Europe and make Europe advance. on the social level, on the defence level, and I hope, on the level of security for Europe's citizens," he said.

"It's not Europe which provoked France's budget difficulties, it's not Maastricht or Brussels which provoked the deficit of our social security system, it's the Socialist deficits (when they were in power)," Barnier said.
